newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil price falls as Iraqi exports loom again.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil price falls as Iraqi exports loom again.

text.p: Oil prices fell on Tuesday after Iraq said it expected to resume oil exports under the United Nations oil-for food deal in seven to 10 days.

International benchmark Brent crude futures closed 11 cents lower at $17.87 as Iraq diverted oil traders' attention away from the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) meeting due to start on Wednesday.
Earlier, Brent had peaked at $18.14 as Saudi Arabia signalled current OPEC production limits should be renewed, as expected, despite flagrant quota-busting.

Prices had risen strongly on Monday on fears a U.N. resolution threatening Iraq with sanctions for blocking arms inspectors, and Baghdad's angry response, would lead to a summer of tension that would hit crude supplies.
The war of words continued on Tuesday with one of Baghdad's most influential newspapers predicting further friction between Iraq and U.N. arms inspectors.

Traders had speculated that that could have resulted in a delay to the second tranche of limited Iraqi oil exports after the first six-month period of the deal expired at the end of May, resulting in tighter supply on the international spot market.

But speaking in Madrid later on Tuesday Iraq's Oil Minster, Amir Rasheed, said: "we expect to start exporting oil in the next week to ten days and we don't anticipate any problems in discussions (with the U.N.)".
"Its the last thing the bulls wanted," said Nigel Saperia, managing director, of the oil division at Bankers Trust International in London.
"Any uncertainty that we could have had is now gone," said Scott Carter, senior oil trader at tosco Petroleum in London.
Oil prices have slumped from close to $25 last year to around $18 for a barrel of North Sea Brent crude and the outlook is still bearish, said traders.
"Its the worst summer in recent memory. The fundamentals are not pretty," said Saperia
Despite a bearish mood among traders, OPEC ministers were eager to put a positive spin on the market.

Saudi Arabian oil minister Ali Naimi said demand for oil was strong enough to soak up OPEC output, currently running two million barrels per day (bpd) above the nominal ceiling of 25.03 million bpd, and to stop prices falling further.
"Demand is good. There is no reason for prices to go lower," said Naimi, who also indicated the energetic over-production of other cartel members would be addressed.
"A rollover is good if everyone adheres to their quota," he said.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, and at eight million bpd the biggest quota holder, is one of the cartel's most restrained producers, despite having two million bpd in spare capacity.
It has given no hint it will abandon its stance and agree to the suggestion of cash-hungry Venezuela, that quotas should be abandoned and price ignored in a dash for market share.
Other OPEC members have called on quota violators to adhere to official allocations.
